::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This guide goes with [meeting 10](../sessions/10-writing.qmd). Use it
for the proposal outline, due November 11, and for the written
proposal, due December 11. The checklist at the end is the one to run
before you submit.
:::

The proposal is graded against the syllabus's [required
headings](../syllabus.qmd#what-you-are-graded-against), and two
questions move a grade more than anything else: is the claim in the
first sentence, and could it come out the other way? This guide is
about the rest: who reads your document, in what order, and what keeps
them reading. It has seven principles, the standard order of six kinds
of document, the style rules, and a checklist.

## 1. Know who reads which part

Every document has three kinds of reader, in a mix that depends on the
setting.

| | In research | In an organization |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Skimmers** read the title and the summary, then stop | Someone searching for papers; a student | The executive who needs the big picture |
| **Engaged readers** read the introduction and the main results | Someone writing a literature review; a researcher deciding whether the paper matters to them | The manager who acts on the recommendation |
| **Deep readers** read the methods and the appendix | A peer who follows the work; a critic; a referee | The analyst who checks the numbers |

**Write each part for the reader who reaches it.** The title and the
abstract serve skimmers: no jargon, and no acronyms in the title. The
introduction serves engaged readers: use the field's terms and define
each one at first use. The methods and the appendix serve deep readers
and carry the full technical detail. Some details are never read, and
they are there for the few who need them.

**Your proposal's readers.** The instructor grades it. The grading
standard asks that somebody outside your team could act on it, so
write the first page for that person: the manager, client or data
provider who would use the answer.

**Evidence.** On a National Institutes of Health review panel, about 20
people score each application and three read it closely; the institute
tells applicants to write the summary parts for a reader of *Scientific
American* ([NIAID](https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/know-your-audience)).
People who know something overestimate how much others know, the
*curse of knowledge* ([Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber
1989](https://doi.org/10.1086/261651)).

**The journal sets the framing.** The same research is framed for the
reader of the outlet. Bloom and coauthors' experiment at a Chinese
travel agency appeared in the *Quarterly Journal of Economics* as an
incentive problem, whether employees shirk at home ([Bloom, Liang,
Roberts and Ying 2015](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qju032)). A later
experiment at the same firm appeared in *Nature* as a management
practice that about 100 million employees in Europe and North America
have adopted ([Bloom, Han and Liang 2024](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07500-2)).

## 2. Nest the versions for those readers

The title, the abstract, the introduction and the full paper are four
versions of one message, nested like Russian dolls. Each one carries
the whole message at its own length and its reader's technical level.
The repetition is intended, and each version rewords the one before
([Doumont 2002](https://doi.org/10.1109/TPC.2002.805164)).

**Keep the feature that identifies the paper.** A title that fits a
dozen papers tells a skimmer nothing. *Climate change and global
agricultural productivity* is a topic. *Anthropogenic climate change
has slowed global agricultural productivity growth* is a finding, and
it fits one paper ([Ortiz-Bobea et al.
2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-021-01000-1)).

**One study, three titles.** The same 2021 study appeared as:

- *The Historical Impact of Anthropogenic Climate Change on Global
  Agricultural Productivity*, a working paper for economists
  ([arXiv 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.10415));
- *Anthropogenic climate change has slowed global agricultural
  productivity growth*, in a journal read by scientists in many fields;
- *Climate change has cost 7 years of ag productivity growth*, in the
  university's news story for the public ([Cornell Chronicle
  2021](https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2021/04/climate-change-has-cost-7-years-ag-productivity-growth)).

**Lengths.** A title runs about ten words. Economics journals cap
abstracts at 100 words (the [*American Economic
Review*](https://www.aeaweb.org/journals/aer/submissions) and the
[*Journal of Finance*](https://afajof.org/submission-guidelines/)) or
150 (*[Econometrica](https://www.econometricsociety.org/publications/econometrica/information-authors)*),
about five sentences: the question, the data and design, the finding
with its size, and what it means. Readers stop early: US internists
reported reading only the abstract for 63% of the articles they read
([Saint et al. 2000](https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1525-1497.2000.00202.x)).

**In your proposal** the versions are the title, the first page and
the full document. Organizations build the same layers on purpose: the
US Government Accountability Office publishes every report as Fast
Facts, a two-page Highlights and the full report.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Practice: your project's four versions

Write a title that states your question (about ten words), one sentence
that states the question and how you will answer it, a 100-word
abstract, and the first paragraph of your introduction. Show the title
alone to someone outside your team and ask what the project is. If
they cannot say, the title is missing its tail.
:::

## 3. Use the structure readers expect

Experienced readers know where each part of a document sits. Twelve
researchers given shuffled paragraphs from articles in their field put
82.6% back in the right section ([Dillon
1991](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0020-7373(05)80168-3)). Follow the
standard order, so the reader finds each part where they look for it.

### An empirical economics paper

1. **Title.** States the finding.
2. **Abstract.** The question, the data and design, the finding with
   its size.
3. **Introduction.** The funnel to the question, the finding and its
   size, the two or three closest papers and what is new.
4. **Setting and data.** Where and when, and what one row describes.
5. **Empirical strategy.** The design and its identifying assumption:
   what must hold for the estimate to measure the effect.
6. **Results.** Each table introduced by its point.
7. **Threats to validity.** What could break the design, and the
   checks.
8. **Conclusion.** The message again, shorter.

Sources: [Dudenhefer
2014](https://econ.duke.edu/sites/econ.duke.edu/files/file-attachments/Dudenhefer,%20Paul%20-%20Guide%20to%20Writing%20in%20Economics.pdf);
[Head, *The Introduction
Formula*](https://blogs.ubc.ca/khead/research/research-advice/formula).

### A paper with a theory section

Some applied papers open with a model, which says what the data must
deliver. The theoretical framework comes right after the introduction,
and its main prediction maps one to one onto the empirical framework
([Bellemare 2018](https://marcfbellemare.com/wordpress/12797)).

1. **Title, abstract and introduction.** As above, with the model's
   prediction in the abstract.
2. **Theoretical framework.** A model that yields the testable
   prediction.
3. **Empirical framework.** The regression for each part of the
   prediction.
4. **Data.** And descriptive statistics.
5. **Results.** Each estimate read back through the model.
6. **Conclusion.**

Example: [Ortiz-Bobea (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajae/aaz047)
values farmland as farming income plus the option to convert it to
other uses. The model predicts that farmland prices and cash rents give
the same climate effect only where conversion is unlikely, and the
empirical sections estimate the effect from each and compare them. In
your proposal, the conceptual model heading plays this role.

### The research proposal for this course

Your proposal is a plan: about five pages that someone could pick up
and execute in January. Page one answers three questions that any
funder asks: *What are we going to learn that we do not know now? Why
is it worth knowing? How will we know that the conclusions are valid?*
Przeworski and Salomon wrote them for applicants to fellowships of the
Social Science Research Council, a US funder of social science
([Przeworski and
Salomon](https://law.uga.edu/sites/default/files/OnTheArtOfWritingProposals_SocialScienceResearchCouncilCompetiotions.pdf)).
Preliminary evidence is optional; use it only to show that the data
exist and can answer the question. The sections follow the course's
required headings, from the syllabus, in this order:

1. Research problem
2. Practical justification
3. What is already known
4. Conceptual model
5. Methodological approach
6. Study sample
7. Data and access
8. Internal validity
9. External validity
10. Limitations and self-critique
11. Work plan
12. Research ethics
13. References

In the outline, each heading becomes topic sentences in order, with
the evidence listed under each.

### A policy or business memo

1. **Subject line.** States the bottom line.
2. **Bottom line.** The conclusion and the decision asked for, in the
   first sentence.
3. **Background.** Only what this reader needs.
4. **Evidence.** Most important first.
5. **Options and risks.**
6. **Next steps.**

US Navy officers read memos written bottom line first, with short
paragraphs, headings and plain sentences, 17–23% faster than memos in
a bureaucratic style, and understood them better ([Suchan and Colucci
1989](https://doi.org/10.1177/0893318989002004002)).

### An executive summary

1. **The issue.** What the reader faces.
2. **The answers.** What the work found, as numbers.
3. **What it means for this reader.** The decision it informs.
4. **Background.** Only what the answers need.
5. **The approach.** In a line or two.

The Canadian Health Services Research Foundation asked for 1:3:25: one
page of main messages, a three-page executive summary and at most 25
pages of report.

### A research talk

1. **Motivation.** Why anybody should care, in the first thirty seconds.
2. **The question.**
3. **What this work does.**
4. **A preview of the findings.**
5. **Data.**
6. **Design.**
7. **Results.**
8. **The bottom line, as a number.**

Meeting 12 covers talks in full.

### The funnel

The first paragraph of an introduction or a proposal is a funnel. It
moves from the field to your question in a few sentences: why it
matters, what is known, what is missing, and the question. In the 2021
paper, the first paragraph runs from why agricultural productivity
matters to the sentence *the impacts of this ACC on the agricultural
sector have not yet been quantified*, and paragraph 3 opens with the
question. In your proposal, the top of the funnel is the decision your
reader faces.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Practice: a five-line memo

Turn your project description into a memo of five lines to the person
who would act on the answer: the subject line, the bottom line, the
one fact of background they need, the evidence you will produce, and
the decision it will inform.
:::

## 4. Write one idea per paragraph

A **topic sentence** states the paragraph's point, and the other
sentences support it. Body paragraphs open with their point, so a
reader who reads only first sentences gets the argument. The opening
funnel of an introduction is the one paragraph that ends with its
point.

**Check a draft with a reverse outline.** Meeting 5 wrote the outline
before the prose. The reverse outline runs the same tool on a draft:

1. Read each paragraph and write one sentence that states what it
   argues.
2. If a paragraph needs two sentences, it holds two ideas. Split it.
3. If the sentence you wrote matches a later sentence in the paragraph,
   the point is buried. Move that sentence to the front.
4. Read your sentences in order. If they make the argument, the draft
   works. If one is hard to write, that paragraph has no point yet.

**Example.** Ray and coauthors close a study of ten crops with a
paragraph whose first sentence is its point: *Our findings here
illustrate that climate change has potentially already affected global
production of the ten largest crops and the production of consumable
food calories in specific countries and globally.* The next three
sentences give the approach, the size and the use ([Ray et al.
2019](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0217148)).

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Practice: reverse-outline your project description

Write one sentence for each paragraph of your October 23 project
description. Read the sentences in order and mark the paragraphs whose
sentence was hard to write. Those are the paragraphs to rewrite first
for the outline.
:::

## 5. Keep the reader on your path

You decide what the reader reads and in what order. What the reader
thinks along the way is up to the reader. Writing is a walk with your
reader along a path you lay, and readers leave it. In laboratory
studies, readers' minds wandered 20 to 30% of the time, and more
wandering went with lower comprehension ([D'Mello and Mills
2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/lnc3.12412); [Bonifacci et al.
2023](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02141-w)). Skeptical readers
argue back as they read.

An **off-ramp** is a point where a doubt pulls the reader off your
path. An **on-ramp** is a "you are here" sign: one sentence at the start
of a section that tells a reader who drifted where the section fits in
the whole argument.

| | Off the path | Solution |
|:-|:--|:--|
| 1 | **A criticism of the design** | Answer it briefly in the sentence after the claim that raises it, and point to the full check |
| 2 | **A variation** the reader wonders about | Say which cases the design covers |
| 3 | **A limitation** on where the result applies | State it yourself, once, in the limitations section |
| 4 | **A reader who drifted** | Open each section with a "you are here" sentence: how it fits in the overall argument |

**Example.** A proposal for the solar project says developers often
build on cheap farmland at the edge of a village. A skeptical reader
asks at once whether prices there were already growing more slowly.
The next sentence answers it, briefly: *Section 4 checks whether
prices there were already growing more slowly.* One short sentence is
enough. Name the doubt and point to where the paper handles it, as
robustness checks usually do, and leave the full answer for its own
section. Outside advertising, raising an objection and refuting it persuades
slightly more than leaving it out, and raising it without refuting it
persuades less ([O'Keefe
1999](https://doi.org/10.1080/23808985.1999.11678963)). In news stories
about cancer research, readers trusted the scientists more when the
story reported limitations, and most when the scientists stated them
([Jensen 2008](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2958.2008.00324.x)).

**Where readers drift.** The data section, with its sources, filters
and merges, loses the most readers. Open it by restating the question,
saying what kind of data the question needs and why, and only then say
where the data come from and what you do to them. For the solar project:
*to learn whether a new solar farm lowers the prices of nearby homes, we
need the sale prices of homes near and far from each farm, before and
after it opens; county averages would mix the two groups, so we need
each sale with its address and date.* Then the source and the
filters. After their minds wander, readers usually go back a
line or two ([Varao-Sousa, Solman and Kingstone
2017](https://doi.org/10.1037/cep0000123)), so put the summary where
they will land: at the start of each section and in the first sentence
of each paragraph. The same holds in talks, most of all long ones: at each new part,
say where it fits in the argument.

**Proofread.** A spelling error is an off-ramp of a cruder kind. On
Kickstarter, projects with spelling errors reached their funding goal
less often ([Mollick
2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusvent.2013.06.005)). Have someone
outside the team read the final draft.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Practice: read your draft as a skeptic

Next to each claim in your draft, write the question a skeptical
reader would ask: a criticism, a variation or a limitation. Then check
whether the next sentence answers it. If it does not, either answer it
there or move it to the limitations section.
:::

## 6. Write plain, neutral sentences

Academic and professional prose gets a true claim to the reader with
the least effort. Each rule below has a before and an after; the
examples are hypothetical unless a source is given.

1. **Active voice**, with *we* for the team. *Sale records were
   obtained from ATTOM* becomes *We obtained sale records from ATTOM*.
   Use the passive only when the actor does not matter.
2. **Present tense** for what a paper or table shows, past for what
   happened in its sample, future for your plans.
   *Gaur and Lang (2023) found that solar farms lower home values*
   becomes *Gaur and Lang (2023) find that homes in Massachusetts and
   Rhode Island within 0.6 miles of a solar farm lost 1.5 to 3.6
   percent of their value*
   ([Gaur and Lang 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2023.106699)).
   The present tense goes on the paper's verb, never on the finding
   about its sample.
3. **Verbs** in place of nominalizations, nouns made from verbs. *We
   conduct an analysis of sale prices* becomes *We analyze sale
   prices*.
4. **One term** for one thing. *Solar farm, array, facility and
   project* in one paragraph read as four things. McCloskey cites a
   paper that used eight terms for one idea in two pages ([McCloskey
   1985](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1465-7295.1985.tb01761.x), rule 19).
5. **Name the study** and its setting. *The literature finds that solar
   farms lower home values* becomes *Elmallah et al. (2023) find that,
   across more than 1,500 solar projects in six states, homes within
   half a mile sold for about 1.5 percent less than homes two to four
   miles away* ([Elmallah et al.
   2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enpol.2023.113425)).
6. **Hedge once**, on the interpretation, where the doubt lies. State
   what the data show plainly. *Visits may have fallen somewhat more,
   which possibly suggests the boycott may have mattered* becomes
   *Visits fell 2.1 percent more in the most Republican third of
   counties. The gap may reflect the boycott, or a local shock in the
   same weeks.* (The 2.1 percent is invented.)
7. **The number in place of the adjective.** *Target's sales collapsed
   dramatically* becomes *comparable store sales fell 4.3 percent in
   the second quarter of 2023* ([Target
   2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/27419/000002741923000032/a2023q2ex-99.htm)).
   Give the number, its unit, the comparison and the period.
8. **No hype words**, the adjectives and adverbs that praise the work:
   novel, first, groundbreaking, critical, very, clearly. Say once what
   is new, compared with the closest published study. You need not
   write "the first study to": an introduction that shows the gap makes
   that plain, and some journals remove such claims before acceptance
   ([*Nature Human Behaviour*
   2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-021-01068-x)).
9. **Short words and no throat-clearing.** Cut *it should be noted
   that* and *it is important to mention*. Follow every *this* with its
   noun.

**When to cite.** Cite any claim a reader could dispute: a number,
another study's finding, a method you borrow. Common knowledge needs no
citation. Mark a hypothesis or an opinion as yours (*we expect*, *we
argue*) and cite the evidence behind it, if any. Point your own results
to the table or figure that shows them. The test is whether a
reasonable reader could ask "says who?".

**Why hype words fail.** In the abstracts of grants funded by NIH, the
share with at least one hype word rose from 72% in 1985 to 97% in
2020, so the words no longer tell a reviewer which work is new ([Millar,
Batalo and Budgell 2022](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2022.28676)).
Promotional words did go with higher odds of funding in one study of
11,535 applications, but the data are observational, and a reviewer
cannot check *novel* without a comparison ([Qiu et al.
2024](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.48696)).

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Practice: five sentences to rewrite

Each sentence breaks at least one rule above. Rewrite it, then open the
suggested answer below.

1. A novel and comprehensive analysis of boycott effects was conducted
   by our team.
2. Store visits may have possibly declined somewhat following the 2023
   boycott.
3. The literature shows that boycotts hurt retailers.
4. Solar arrays, PV facilities and solar projects all affect nearby
   homes, and these installations are growing.
5. It should be noted that this is very important for planning boards.

**Suggested answers.** (1) We estimate how much store visits fell after
each boycott. (2) Store visits fell 2.1 percent in the 20 weeks after
the 2023 boycott, against the same weeks a year earlier (the number is
invented; give yours). (3) Name the study, its setting and its number,
for example the Target earnings release on comparable store sales. (4)
Pick one term, *solar farm*, and use it every time; give the growth as
a number with its source. (5) Say who decides what: town planning
boards set how far solar farms must sit from homes.
:::

## 7. Write in three passes

A paper is written from the big picture down to the sentence, the way
meeting 5 asked you to plan code. There are three passes, and each
starts only when the one before it is finished.

1. **Sections.** List the headings the document needs, in order. For
   the proposal they are the thirteen required headings. For a paper,
   start from the schematic in section 3.
2. **Outline.** Under each heading, write one bullet per paragraph.
   Each bullet holds the topic sentence, written out in full, and the
   evidence the paragraph will point to: the citation, the number, the
   table or figure. The outline is exhaustive, so every paragraph of the
   draft has its bullet. If you cannot write the bullet, the paragraph
   has no point yet. The proposal outline due November 11 is this pass.
3. **Prose.** Turn each bullet into a paragraph. Open with the bullet's
   point, answer each doubt in the sentence that follows it, open each
   section with a "you are here" sentence, and use precise terms and
   numbers throughout. Do not bury the point at the end of the
   paragraph.

**The outline sets the length.** Plan about 150 words a paragraph. The
number of bullets then gives the length of the draft. If the count runs
past the page limit, cut bullets, which means cutting points, before
you write any prose. Trimming words from finished paragraphs costs more
time and saves less space.

**An example.** The main text of the 2021 paper on climate change and
farm productivity, in the version first submitted ([Ortiz-Bobea et al.
2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.10415)), has sixteen paragraphs. The
journal prints no headings in the main text, but the outline behind it
had seven sections. The slides for meeting 10 rebuild that outline
bullet by bullet. Here is its length.

| Section | Paragraphs | At 150 words each | Words written |
|:--------|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| Introduction | 3 | 450 | 357 |
| Framework and model | 2 | 300 | 322 |
| Data | 1 | 150 | 113 |
| How productivity responds to weather | 3 | 450 | 448 |
| Impact of climate change since 1961 | 3 | 450 | 315 |
| Checks | 3 | 450 | 437 |
| Caveats and conclusion | 1 | 150 | 272 |
| **Total** | **16** | **2,400** | **2,264** |

Twelve of the sixteen paragraphs state their point in the first
sentence. The other four show the usual exceptions: the opening funnel
ends on its point, a paragraph that sets up an equation states its
point after it, a paragraph that opens with a question answers it in
sentence 4, and the last paragraph carries three points that an outline
would have given three bullets.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Practice: outline your proposal

Write the proposal's thirteen headings. Under each, write one bullet
per paragraph: the topic sentence in full, then the evidence it will
point to. Count the bullets, multiply by 150, and compare the total
with the page limit. Cut bullets until it fits, then read the topic
sentences alone, in order. They should give the argument.
:::

## Checklist before you submit

Run it on the outline on November 11, and again on the proposal.

- [ ] The title states your question, or your finding, in about ten
      words, with no acronyms.
- [ ] Page one answers the three questions: what we will learn, why it
      is worth knowing, and how we will know the answer is right.
- [ ] The first paragraph is a short funnel that ends on your question.
- [ ] The sections follow the thirteen required headings, in order.
- [ ] The outline has a bullet for every paragraph, with its topic
      sentence and its evidence.
- [ ] Every paragraph opens with its point, except the opening funnel.
      The reverse outline reads as the argument.
- [ ] Each objection a skeptical reader would raise is answered next to
      the claim that raises it, or stated once in the limitations
      section.
- [ ] Each section opens with a "you are here" sentence on how it fits
      the argument.
- [ ] Every technical term is defined at first use, and each thing has
      one name throughout.
- [ ] Every claim about size is a number with its unit, its comparison
      and its period.
- [ ] Every study is named with its setting, and nothing is attributed
      to "the literature".
- [ ] Every claim a reader could dispute has a source, and every
      hypothesis or opinion is marked as yours.
- [ ] No hype words. What is new is stated once, against the closest
      published study.
- [ ] Someone outside the team has read it for spelling and for sense.

## Further reading

- Mensh and Kording (2017), [*Ten simple rules for structuring
  papers*](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005619). Short and
  free.
- Przeworski and Salomon (1988, rev. 1995), [*On the Art of Writing
  Proposals*](https://law.uga.edu/sites/default/files/OnTheArtOfWritingProposals_SocialScienceResearchCouncilCompetiotions.pdf).
  What a proposal's reader looks for.
- Gopen and Swan (1990), [*The Science of Scientific
  Writing*](https://www.jstor.org/stable/29774235), American Scientist
  78(6). Readers look for information where they expect to find it.
- McCloskey (1985), [*Economical
  Writing*](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1465-7295.1985.tb01761.x),
  Economic Inquiry 23(2). A style guide written by an economist for
  economists.
